## **2\. Product Background** {#2.-product-background}

Electrical infrastructure inspection is important for identifying visible defects in assets such as towers, conductors, insulators, and associated equipment. Conventional inspection may require substantial field effort, while UAV-based image collection can support safer observation and more systematic documentation of asset conditions.

UAV inspection produces images and other evidence that must be organized, reviewed, associated with inspection activities and assets, and followed up when defects are confirmed. When mission records, visual evidence, AI results, and maintenance information are handled separately, tracking the status and history of an inspection becomes more difficult.

Publicly documented initiatives demonstrate the relevance of UAV and AI technology to power-grid inspection in Vietnam. EVN reported recognition of a UAV/AI initiative developed by Quang Tri Power Company [\[1\]](#bookmark=id.y4og6liklhpl), and EVNCPC has published information on UAV-based inspection and AI-related development [\[2\]](#bookmark=id.urlezejk14yu). These cases are used as background references; they do not establish an enterprise requirement or partnership for this capstone.

UAV-PMS is independently proposed and developed by the student team as an academic capstone project. It is not commissioned, sponsored, or formally validated by EVN, EVNSPC, EVNCPC, or their affiliated units. The team defines and evaluates its own prototype requirements, focusing on inspection mission management, AI-assisted defect detection, emergency alerts, GIS-based visualization, evidence review, and maintenance follow-up.

## **3\. Existing Systems** {#3.-existing-systems}

### **3.1 QTPC UAV AI Distribution Grid Inspection System** {#3.1-qtpc-uav-ai-distribution-grid-inspection-system}

**Description:** Quang Tri Power Company (QTPC) reports a UAV, Internet of Things (IoT), and AI system for inspecting distribution-grid assets and warning of safety risks. Its June 2026 presentation describes an inspection workflow, a flight-control application, a central WebApp, AI services, and interfaces to internal EVN/EVNCPC systems [\[3\]](#bookmark=id.umqfy0qomm90).  
**Actors:** QTPC's workflow shows managers using the Web client, field staff or drone operators using the mobile and flight-control applications, and technical staff reviewing AI results and inspection records.Inferred from the documented workflow. [\[3\]](#bookmark=id.umqfy0qomm90)  
**Features:** The documented workflow covers inspection planning and route selection, UAV data capture, image and flight-history storage, AI-assisted detection and warning, technical review of findings, GIS or map views, inspection forms, and API connections to internal systems [\[3\]](#bookmark=id.umqfy0qomm90). The report describes visible-light and thermal inspection modes.  
**Pros:** QTPC's system connects flight planning, UAV inspection, AI-assisted detection, technical review, and inspection records in one operational process. It also provides GIS views, flight history, and asset information for grid inspection. The reported pilot inspected more than 180 km of power lines, demonstrating use in a Vietnamese electricity operation [\[3\]](#bookmark=id.umqfy0qomm90).   
**Cons:** The inspection workflow passes approved results to PMIS/KTHT for subsequent handling, so presentation shows approved results being passed to PMIS/KTHT with other systems rather than being shown as a complete maintenance lifecycle within this system [\[3\]](#bookmark=id.umqfy0qomm90). QTPC also reports that image storage must be upgraded for shared use and a more powerful GPU is needed for wider deployment [\[3\]](#bookmark=id.umqfy0qomm90). 

### **3.2 Optelos Power Utility Inspection Platform**  {#3.2-optelos-power-utility-inspection-platform}

**Description:** Optelos is a platform for managing power-utility inspections, from scheduling and drone data intake to AI analysis and maintenance action.  
**Actors:** Utility inspection managers, drone pilots or contractors, analysts reviewing defects, and teams dispatched to investigate them [\[4\]](#bookmark=id.17k4p57ujpav).  
**Features:** Job scheduling and tracking; drone image and video intake; data quality checks; AI-assisted identification of assets and defects; geolocated findings; reports; and trouble tickets linked to repair dispatch [\[4\]](#bookmark=id.17k4p57ujpav).  
**Pros:** Optelos connects inspection evidence, defect location, prioritization, and follow-up action in one workflow. Its published functions include both scheduling and ticketing, making it a strong reference for those parts of UAV-PMS [\[4\]](#bookmark=id.17k4p57ujpav).  
**Cons:** The workflow depends on uploading data to a central vendor platform and connecting it with a utility’s existing GIS, ticketing, or asset-management systems. Adopting the complete workflow therefore requires data-transfer and integration arrangements [\[4\]](#bookmark=id.17k4p57ujpav).

### **3.3 Hepta Insights Power-Line Inspection Platform** {#3.3-hepta-insights-power-line-inspection-platform}

**Description:** Hepta Insights is an AI-assisted platform focused on inspecting power lines and reviewing the condition of grid assets.  
**Actors:** Grid operators, qualified inspectors, engineering teams, managers, and maintenance crews [\[5\]](#bookmark=id.yt8073ra4jh9).  
Features: Aggregation of RGB, infrared, and LiDAR data; asset-based digital models; AI-assisted defect screening; inspector review; cloud access to inspection data; PDF/XLS reports; and integration with customer workflows [\[5\]](#bookmark=id.yt8073ra4jh9).  
**Pros:** Hepta is purpose-built for power-grid inspection. It brings together several image and sensor types, links findings to assets, and retains a human review step before inspection results inform decisions [\[5\]](#bookmark=id.yt8073ra4jh9).  
**Cons:** Hepta states that its specialized AI models are based on customer asset data and that inspection data is made available through its cloud platform. A utility must therefore provide suitable data and establish the necessary data and system integrations to use these capabilities effectively [\[5\]](#bookmark=id.yt8073ra4jh9).

### **3.4 Skydio 3D Scan** {#3.4-skydio-3d-scan}

**Description:** Skydio 3D Scan is software for planning autonomous drone flights and capturing images of physical assets. UAV-PMS uses it as a reference for the flight-planning and image-collection stages, not as a power-line inspection management system.  
**Actors:** Drone operators and inspection or surveying teams responsible for defining the capture area, conducting flights, and reviewing the collected images [\[6\]](#bookmark=id.h71nbafmk3i0).  
**Features:** The operator defines an area or asset to capture. The software plans a flight path that adapts to the asset’s geometry, controls image coverage and overlap, supports repeatable capture, and lets the team review coverage before exporting images for further processing [\[6\]](#bookmark=id.h71nbafmk3i0).  
**Pros:** Adaptive flight planning and coverage review help teams collect consistent images of complex structures. These functions are useful references when designing how UAV-PMS plans inspection flights and checks whether sufficient visual evidence was captured [\[6\]](#bookmark=id.h71nbafmk3i0).  
**Cons:** Skydio 3D Scan focuses on flight execution and data capture. The workflow described for this product does not cover power-grid defect classification, confirmation of findings, or maintenance follow-up. UAV-PMS therefore needs its own processes for those stages after images have been collected [\[6\]](#bookmark=id.h71nbafmk3i0).

### **3.5 DJI Matrice 30T and Pilot 2 Powerline Inspection**  {#3.5-dji-matrice-30t-and-pilot-2-powerline-inspection}

**Description:** DJI Enterprise offers drone, camera, flight-planning, and data-management solutions for inspecting transmission and distribution lines.  
**Actors:** Drone pilots, inspection staff, remote-operation staff, and personnel who review inspection images and reports [\[7\]](#bookmark=id.h8qfn5npubmy).  
**Features:** DJI describes waypoint-based or scheduled inspection missions, reusable flight routes, visual and thermal image capture, and data management through products such as DJI Pilot 2 and FlightHub 2\. Available functions depend on the selected drone, camera, dock, and software configuration [\[7\]](#bookmark=id.h8qfn5npubmy).  
**Pros:** The Matrice 30T and DJI Pilot 2 support waypoint missions that can be saved and repeated for subsequent power-line inspections. The drone captures both visual and thermal images, giving inspectors evidence of visible conditions and abnormal equipment temperatures [\[7\]](#bookmark=id.h8qfn5npubmy).  
**Cons:** In the Matrice 30T workflow described by DJI, inspectors analyze the captured photographs manually to identify and locate defects. Inspection data must then be connected to an asset-management system for further analysis and maintenance planning [\[7\]](#bookmark=id.h8qfn5npubmy).

## **4\. Business Opportunity** {#4.-business-opportunity}

The project addresses a software engineering opportunity to integrate inspection planning, UAV-collected evidence, AI-assisted defect analysis, and maintenance follow-up in a single prototype workflow. The motivation is based on the team’s study of the inspection domain and existing products, rather than on a formally assigned enterprise project.

The reference systems reviewed above provide examples of flight planning, asset inspection, AI analysis, geospatial visualization, and maintenance coordination. UAV-PMS brings selected capabilities together for an academic demonstration, with a team-developed UAV prototype, lightweight Edge AI for time-sensitive detection, and server-side AI for more detailed post-flight processing.

The expected value of the capstone is a demonstrable and testable end-to-end workflow, not a claim of deployment readiness or measurable business benefits for a specific electricity utility. Its feasibility will be assessed through software testing, model evaluation, controlled demonstrations, and clearly labeled sample or simulated operational data where real enterprise records are unavailable.

## **5\. Software Product Vision** {#5.-software-product-vision}

For inspection managers, UAV operators, and maintenance personnel who need to coordinate inspection activities and review potential infrastructure defects, UAV-PMS is an independently developed prototype platform that connects UAV inspection records, AI-assisted visual analysis, geographic context, and maintenance follow-up.

The system supports mission planning and assignment, asset and evidence management, two AI processing modes (Edge AI and Server AI), human validation of detection results, emergency alert handling, GIS monitoring, and maintenance ticket tracking. It aims to improve traceability across these steps within a controlled capstone environment.

Unlike a standalone object detector or drone flight-control application, UAV-PMS demonstrates how detection outputs can be incorporated into a broader inspection and maintenance workflow. Its functionality and performance will be validated within the available prototype and test conditions, without claiming integration into an operational utility environment.

## **6\. Project Scope & Limitations** {#6.-project-scope-&-limitations}

### **6.1 Major Features** {#6.1-major-features}

• **FE-01:** Mission Management – create, assign, approve where applicable, track, and close routine inspection missions; support administrative completion of urgent field activities without making the alerting mechanism dependent on prior mission approval.  
• **FE-02:** UAV Prototype Integration – demonstrate image capture or data acquisition using the team-developed UAV and connect available inspection evidence to the software workflow.  
• **FE-03:** Hybrid AI Defect Detection – lightweight Edge AI for time-sensitive detection and server-side AI for post-flight analysis; the current six-class taxonomy is insulator, insulator\_broken, insulator\_flashover, bird\_nest, foreign\_object, and broken\_strand.  
• **FE-04:** Detection Review – display defect labels, bounding boxes, confidence values, evidence, and validation status for human review.  
• **FE-05:** GIS Monitoring – visualize sample or imported assets, inspection activities, and associated findings using Leaflet; clearly distinguish simulated asset locations from verified real-world coordinates.  
• **FE-06:** Emergency Alerts – accept device-originated critical detections even when a mission has not yet been approved or assigned; route notifications to configured management or duty personnel, subject to connectivity and available device identity.  
• **FE-07:** Maintenance Follow-up – create and track maintenance tickets from validated findings, including assignment and status changes.  
• **FE-08:** Reporting and Analytics – provide inspection summaries and export supported records in available formats.

***Figure 1\.** Feature Tree For The UAV-PMS System.*

### **6.2 Limitations & Exclusions** {#6.2-limitations-&-exclusions}

• **LI-1:** The UAV is a student-built prototype and is not a certified commercial inspection platform. Field demonstrations are subject to safety, legal, and practical constraints.  
• **LI-2:** The system does not carry out physical maintenance or repair and does not replace professional inspection or engineering decisions.  
• **LI-3:** Aviation permissions, pilot licensing, and beyond-visual-line-of-sight operations are not provided by the software.  
• **LI-4:** No direct integration with EVN/EVNSPC/EVNCPC enterprise systems, SCADA, PMIS, or KTHT is included.  
• **LI-5:** The six-class defect taxonomy is limited to the available dataset. Detection performance outside the evaluated image distributions, environmental conditions, and hardware configurations is not guaranteed.  
• **LI-6:** GIS may be tested using clearly labeled simulated routes, assets, and locations. Accurate real-world defect geolocation requires verified GPS, asset linkage, or other supporting spatial information; UAV camera position alone does not establish exact defect coordinates.  
• **LI-7:** Immediate remote emergency notification depends on network connectivity. Offline detections may require local buffering and later synchronization.  
• **LI-8:** The prototype does not guarantee identification of the individual UAV operator during urgent dispatch if the handover or assignment has not been recorded electronically.  
• **LI-9:** The first release is an academic prototype, not a production-ready or nationwide deployment.  
• **LI-10:** Long-term asset health index calculation, predictive asset degradation modeling, and lifecycle asset replacement forecasting are excluded from the capstone scope to prioritize the end-to-end field inspection and maintenance ticketing workflow. 

# **III. Research Objectives** {#iii.-research-objectives}

## **1\. General Objective** {#1.-general-objective}

To evaluate the effect of dataset quality curation on UAV-image-based electrical infrastructure defect detection, compare representative YOLO and RT-DETR object detectors under a consistent benchmark, and examine their accuracy–efficiency trade-offs for potential Edge and Server use.

## **2\. Specific Objectives** {#2.-specific-objectives}

The specific objectives of this study are:

1. Integrate and harmonize UAV-based electrical infrastructure image datasets into a consistent six-class detection taxonomy.  
2. Define and document data-quality inspection and curation procedures, including annotation review and appropriate safeguards against data leakage.  
3. Compare selected YOLO and RT-DETR configurations using consistent data splits, training conditions, and evaluation metrics.  
4. Compare raw and curated training conditions to assess the effect of data quality on detection accuracy, class-level results, and localization behavior.  
5. Analyze performance and inference characteristics relevant to resource-constrained Edge and more capable Server environments.  
6. Report limitations, failure cases, and conditions under which findings can and cannot be generalized.

## **3\. Scope and Limitations of Study** {#3.-scope-and-limitations-of-study}

The research focuses on object detection from UAV imagery using a unified six-class dataset: insulator, insulator\_broken, insulator\_flashover, bird\_nest, foreign\_object, and broken\_strand. The benchmark compares selected YOLO and RT-DETR models using common evaluation metrics, including precision, recall, F1-score, mAP, and inference characteristics where measurable.

Experiments examine data preparation and curation as well as differences between model architectures and sizes. A fixed held-out test set should be preserved for final comparison, and any data leakage checks or annotation interventions must be documented. The research component is separate from the capstone software workflow, although its results may inform model selection for the prototype.

The conclusions are constrained by the sources and quality of the available datasets, label consistency, computational resources, and experimental settings. Full-scale validation on operational 110 kV lines, access to official utility GIS records, and certified real-world UAV inspection are outside the research scope.

## **4\. Significance of the Study** {#4.-significance-of-the-study}

The study provides an empirical comparison of how data curation and detector selection affect electrical infrastructure defect detection in UAV imagery. It is intended to produce reproducible observations about dataset quality, model performance, and computational trade-offs rather than to claim a new detection architecture.

The results may inform future development of AI-assisted inspection tools and the selection of Edge or Server inference approaches. Any practical benefit remains conditional on further validation with representative operational data and human review.
